screening_results.reason: This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related body perception task probing perception/understanding of self and others. The sample comprises healthy adults (N=30, mean age 26, 15 males/15 females) meeting the age/sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and contrasts (e.g., own body > scrambled, same-sex other > scrambled, opposite-sex other > scrambled), thresholded and cluster-corrected, with tables/figures and coordinate reporting. Results for the healthy control participants are reported separately for males and females and in combined analyses, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, age out of range, or missing healthy-group whole-brain maps) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social processing (understanding others' regret) in healthy adult participants (two samples of 24 adults, ages within 18–65). It uses whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (SPM) with group-level contrasts and conjunctions (IP−IF and OP−OF) and reports thresholded statistical maps and activation coordinates; results are described for the healthy/control group. The task is explicitly social (perception/understanding of others' emotional states). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This study uses task fMRI with a social incentive delay paradigm and includes a healthy adult control group (24 HCs aged 19–36), satisfying I3 and I4. However, it does not provide an unmasked, whole-brain, task-evoked statistical map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The reported whole-brain results are primarily between-group contrasts/interactions (BPD>HC, HC>BPD) and ROI-based findings (amygdala), and the authors explicitly state there were no suprathreshold whole-brain activations in the HCs for several contrasts. Because the paper reports mainly between-group contrasts without an accompanying whole-brain healthy-group task effect, it violates the review’s requirement for a healthy-group whole-brain map (E4). Therefore the study must be excluded.

This study used task-based fMRI to measure neural responses to dynamic social interactions (dyads) in healthy adult participants (N=21, ages 18–35). Group-level whole-brain analyses are described: whole-brain beta maps were generated, whole-brain contrasts were used for localizer ROI definition (interaction > scrambled interaction, bodies > objects, faces > objects, mentalizing > pain), and a whole-brain searchlight analysis was performed and reported. Results include group-level statistical outcomes and descriptions of whole-brain searchlight peaks. Thus the paper meets the requirements for task-based fMRI of social processing in healthy adults and reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked analyses (reported in main text and supplementary materials).

This is an fMRI study of social interaction perception in healthy adult participants (ages 18–34 across experiments). The paper reports group-level whole-brain analyses (surface-based random effects group analysis and whole-brain contrasts with FDR correction) identifying pSTS clusters for interaction > non-interaction, satisfying whole-brain reporting. The tasks probe social-related processing (perception/understanding of others) using task-evoked fMRI. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study of social processing (learning about others’ preference similarity to self) in healthy adults (n=25, mean age 25.1). The task is social (affiliation, perception/understanding of others), and the paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results (multiple contrasts, conjunctions, cluster-corrected activations with MNI coordinates) rather than ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses. Whole-brain results are clearly described in the text and tables/figures. Participants fall within the 18–65 range and healthy-group analyses are reported separately. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This study is not a task-based fMRI investigation of social processing in healthy adults. It uses resting-state fMRI and structural MRI to classify ASD versus controls (multimodal classification), with no task-evoked, group-level whole-brain activation maps reported for a healthy adult group. Participants include ASD and control subjects with a median age of 14.7 years (many under 18), and results are presented as classification metrics rather than healthy-group task contrasts. Therefore it violates criteria requiring task-based whole-brain healthy-group activation maps.

Although this fMRI study uses a social cognition task and includes a healthy (typically developing) adult control group, the paper reports task-based functional connectivity results (ROI-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel connectivity) rather than group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps for the healthy/control group. The review’s eligibility requires an unmasked, voxelwise task activation map (e.g., main effect or within-group contrast) from the healthy group. Because the paper presents only connectivity analyses without reporting a whole-brain task activation map for the healthy group, it meets exclusion criterion E3.

This is an fMRI study using the Cyberball social-ostracism paradigm (a social-related task tapping affiliation/ social processing) in adult undergraduates (mean age ~19.8). The sample includes a healthy subgroup (37/46 with no Axis I disorders) and reports group-level, whole-brain task contrasts (EX–IN and SUP–EX) with voxelwise results and coordinates. Results for the healthy/group-level effects are clearly described (one-sample t-tests and regression using BFNE), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain, group-level task activation maps. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-18–65 sample, or non-empirical) are violated.

Although the study used task-based fMRI with a social-affective cinematic stimulus and included a healthy adult control group (I3 and I4 satisfied), it does not report any group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy/control group. The paper focuses on dynamic connectivity measures (network cohesion index, NCI) and between-group comparisons of connectivity, without providing an unmasked healthy-group whole-brain activation map or coordinate-based task activation results. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E3 (connectivity-only analyses without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map).

This is an fMRI study using a social judgment/feedback task (social acceptance/rejection), includes a healthy adult control group (n=20, mean age ~28) with results reported separately, and presents whole-brain, voxelwise within-group activation maps for the control group (reported in text/figures and cluster-corrected whole-brain analyses). The paper therefore meets the review’s requirements for task type, sample, and whole-brain healthy-group task-evoked results.

This paper reports task-based fMRI of action observation and weight-discrimination (perception of others’ hand actions), which falls squarely under social-related processing (Perception and Understanding of Others). Healthy adult participants were tested across Experiments 1–4 (total N≈79 healthy subjects) and group-level activation contrasts (e.g., ActionOBS–CtrlOBS; Sleeve/NoSleeve contrasts) are presented. Analyses include voxelwise, group-level statistical maps (reported and visualized across the whole brain and specifically the cerebellum; some contrasts are presented at whole-brain level, e.g., NoSleeve–Sleeve FG4 result). Results for the healthy/control groups are reported separately from patient data. Therefore the study meets the fMRI social-task requirement, includes healthy adults, and provides whole-brain, group-level task activation maps (reported in figures/text/tables), satisfying I3, I4, I5 and I6.

This is an fMRI study of physician–patient social interactions in healthy adult participants (N=18). However, the imaging results reported here are based on a priori ROI analyses and regression within those ROIs (mOFC/sgACC, rACC/vmPFC, anterior insula, cACC). The paper does not present an unmasked, group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy group (results are restricted to ROI-based inference and FWE correction within ROIs). Therefore it fails to meet the requirement for whole-brain evidence (I5) and falls under exclusion E2 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Other inclusion criteria (use of fMRI during a social task and healthy adult sample) are met, but the lack of whole-brain group maps requires exclusion.

The study includes an appropriate social-related fMRI task (biological motion perception) and healthy adult controls, but the imaging results are presented primarily as ROI-based analyses (STSp and MT localized per subject) with no clear group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map reported for the healthy/control group. Although the authors performed some whole-brain searches, they do not report an unmasked, group-level healthy-task contrast map (e.g., biological>scrambled) suitable for coordinate-based inclusion. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain evidence (I5) and meets exclusion criterion E2.

Although the study uses fMRI during a social-related task (biological motion perception) and includes healthy adult controls for behavioral testing, the paper reports whole-brain task-evoked fMRI results only for a single patient (SL) scanned postoperatively. The manuscript does not present a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group; comparisons to ‘healthy participants’ reference prior data from other work rather than reported healthy-group maps in this paper. Therefore the key inclusion criterion (I5) for a healthy-group whole-brain task effect is not met. Exclusion criterion E4 (no accompanying unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect) applies.

Although this is a task-based fMRI study of social (mentalizing) processing and includes a healthy adult control group, the paper does not report an unmasked, voxelwise, group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group (e.g., a whole-brain GLM show>no-show map). Analyses are based on spatially constrained ICA component spatial maps and component-level temporal-sorting beta-weights (component-level statistics and group comparisons), not on whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy group. Therefore it fails the requirement for a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map and must be excluded (E4).

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adults (N=20 analyzed; mean age 20.65) that investigates event simulation including social situations and social-cognition processes (mentions theory of mind, trait inference; 41/96 stimuli depict social interactions). The study reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., Imp–Con, Exp–Imp, Ftr–Exp) using SPM random-effects analyses with whole-brain cluster correction and peak coordinates reported; results are clearly from the healthy/control sample. Whole-brain results are presented in text, figures, and coordinate tables. Therefore it meets the inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task activation reporting.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adults (N=22, ages 18–25) using the DISC stimulus set to probe social attribution (a social-related task). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (FRIENDS > WATCH and FRIENDS > SIZE) with FSL-based one-sample t-tests, permutation testing, TFCE and cluster correction, and describes whole-brain activation results. Thus it meets the fMRI social task requirement, includes a healthy adult sample, and provides whole-brain group-level task-evoked statistical maps/results (reported in text/figures/tables). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, out-of-range age, or non-empirical) are violated.

Although the study includes a social perception task using task-related fMRI and reports results for a healthy adult control group, the task-evoked fMRI analysis is reported as an ROI-based analysis (ROI ANOVA) rather than a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper provides whole-brain voxelwise analyses for resting-state seed-based connectivity (task-free fMRI) but not for task-evoked whole-brain maps. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain task activation reporting and meets exclusion criterion E2 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain task results).

This is an empirical fMRI study investigating perception and understanding of others’ actions (force estimation), which falls under social-related processing. The sample comprises healthy adult participants (final N=12; mean age 26), meeting the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and contrast analyses using SPM12 (including conjunctions and SUIT cerebellar analyses); results are described with cluster-level statistics and coordinates. The study is not limited to ROI, connectivity-only, or non-empirical approaches. Therefore it meets the review’s inclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (n=28 naturally-cycling women, ages ~22–24) that used a social perception task (Dynamic Interactive Shape Clips) probing animacy and social relationship attribution. The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked analyses (FRIENDS>SIZE, FRIENDS>WATCH, etc.) using permutation testing and cluster correction, and describes group-level whole-brain statistical maps and voxelwise results. Behavioral and fMRI results for the healthy control group are reported separately and in detail. Thus the study meets the requirements for an fMRI social-related task in healthy adults and provides whole-brain group-level activation results reported in the text and figures/supplementary materials.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social communication (real-time mutual eye contact) in healthy adults (mean age ~21.8). It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (LIVE > REPLAY) with corrected inference and provides tables/figures of activated clusters and interbrain synchronization. Results for the healthy participant group are reported separately and satisfy whole-brain reporting requirements.

Although this is an fMRI study of social processing with a healthy control (non-SPD) group, the paper does not report a clear, unmasked whole-brain group-level task activation map identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. The results mainly present combined-group (SPD + non-SPD) main effects, between-group contrasts/interactions, and ROI/parameter estimate extractions. There is no standalone whole-brain healthy-group task map (within-group control results) presented in the full text; thus the report consists of between-group contrasts and ROI analyses without the required healthy-group whole-brain activation map.

While this is an fMRI study of a social-related task (irony comprehension) that includes a healthy adult control group, the paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain, group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The manuscript reports main effects across ‘study participants’ (combined sample) and between-group contrasts (controls>patients) and refers to previously published control-group results, but it does not provide a standalone healthy-group whole-brain task map in the text/tables/supplement that can be unambiguously attributed to the healthy group. According to the review criteria, reporting only between-group contrasts without an accompanying healthy-group whole-brain task effect requires exclusion (E4).

This is a task-based dual-fMRI hyperscanning study of social interaction (cooperation/competition) in healthy adults (38 participants, mean age 22.4), meeting the sample requirement. The study uses fMRI during an explicit social-related task and reports group-level, whole-brain spatial maps from group-ICA that are related to task conditions via regression and group-level comparisons (paired t-tests), providing whole-brain task-evoked evidence. Results are presented as spatial component maps and condition-related statistics, and group-level effects for healthy participants are clearly reported. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state-only, non-healthy sample) are violated.

This fMRI study used a social-related task (self- and other-reflection), which maps onto perception/understanding of self and others. It included a healthy adult control group (n=21) reported separately. The paper reports within-group, whole-brain voxelwise task activation results for the healthy control group (contrasts self>semantic and other>semantic), with corrected thresholds and descriptions of activations (VMPFC, DMPFC, ACC, PCC, precuneus, etc.), and figures/tables. Whole-brain results are presented (text, figures, supplementary material), not limited to ROIs or connectivity analyses. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study using an action-observation task that examines neural responses to observing others’ risk-taking versus safe actions — a social-cognitive paradigm addressing perception/understanding of others. Participants were healthy adults (undergraduate late adolescents aged 18.0–22.8), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (risk-taking vs safe) using SPM with reported coordinates and statistical maps/figures, and presents results for the healthy/control group. No ROI-only, connectivity-only, resting-state-only, or out-of-range age issues apply. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related task (empathy toward humans and animals) in healthy adults (ages 18–60). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise group-level task contrasts (human > neutral; animal > neutral) analyzed with SPM2 and reports peak coordinates and thresholded results (p<0.05 FWE), plus within-group statistical maps and between-group analyses. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion requirements for whole-brain healthy adult task activation reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, resting-state/connectivity-only, age outside range, or non-empirical) are triggered.

This fMRI study measured neural responses in healthy adult participants (N=18, ages 18–27) while they listened to literary stories and contrasted Mentalizing versus Action content. The design probes social-related processing (mentalizing/theory-of-mind) during a task (story comprehension) and used a Theory-of-Mind localizer to identify mentalizing ROIs. The paper reports group-level whole-brain task contrasts (Mentalizing > Action and Action > Mentalizing) with corrected voxelwise/cluster thresholds and provides cluster locations/activations. Thus the study meets criteria for (I3) social-related fMRI task, (I4) healthy adult sample, (I5) whole-brain group-level task-evoked maps, and (I6) acceptable reporting of whole-brain results.

The study meets the review topic (fMRI of social/attachment processing) and includes healthy adult participants (women aged 22–45). However, the published analyses and significance testing were conducted using an a priori ROI approach with small-volume correction (SVC), and the paper frames results as ‘regions of interest’ findings. There is no clear report of an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) group-level task activation map or whole-brain corrected results independent of ROIs. Because the paper reports only ROI/SVC-based task results rather than an unmasked whole-brain task map, it fails inclusion criterion I5 and must be excluded under E2.

This fMRI study used a task (listening to and rating artistic vs. popular music) that elicited and analyzed social-cognition/ToM and empathy-related activations. Authors explicitly report greater recruitment of default mode network/ToM and cognitive-empathy regions (arMFC, PCC/PC, TP, hippocampus) for artistic music and interpret these as social-cognitive/empathic processing. The sample is healthy adults (male, 18–24), and group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation results are reported with coordinates/tables and cluster-level corrections. Thus the paper provides whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps relevant to social-related processing and satisfies the review’s inclusion criteria.

The study is an fMRI investigation of empathy for pain (a social/’Perception and Understanding of Others’ task) in healthy adult volunteers. It includes a young healthy subgroup (ages 20–30) satisfying the 18–65 sample requirement, and reports group-level, whole-brain task activation maps (pain>no pain and pain>baseline) with results and statistical maps made available (figures/tables and NeuroVault/supplement). Whole-brain voxelwise analyses (one-sample t-tests and second-level contrasts) are reported rather than only ROI/seed/connectivity results. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis objective and inclusion criteria.

While this fMRI study uses a social (mentalizing) task and includes a healthy adult control group (I3, I4), the paper does not report an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map for the healthy/control group. The manuscript’s whole-brain analysis is reported only as a between-group contrast (Controls > ASC) and the within-group findings are reported primarily via ROI analyses. Therefore it lacks a clearly identified healthy-group whole-brain task effect, violating inclusion criterion I5 and falling under exclusion criterion E4.

This study uses task-based fMRI to investigate processing of dynamic emotional facial expressions (a social perception task) and reports whole-brain group-level activation for the healthy/control group (control group simple main effect of dynamic vs static, with corrected whole-brain results and coordinates/figures). The paper includes a separate healthy adult control group (n=13, ages within 18–65) with results reported independently from the ASD group. Whole-brain statistical maps and coordinate tables for the control group are presented. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusions.

This study used task-based fMRI of a social judgment (approachability) task (meets social-related construct). It included a healthy adult control group (adults recruited; controls analyzed separately) and reports within-group/whole-brain task contrasts and activations (social > gender and baseline) with group-level voxelwise analyses and supplementary tables/figures for within-group results. Results are not limited to ROI, connectivity, or between-group contrasts only. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, age outside range, or non-empirical) apply.

Study uses fMRI of facial emotion processing (social task) and reports within-group whole-brain maps for the healthy control group; however, the participant age range reported is 16–35 and controls were age-matched to that sample. Inclusion criterion I4 requires at least one group of healthy adult participants aged 18–65. Because the healthy/control group includes participants younger than 18 (min age 16) and no adult-only healthy subgroup is reported separately, the study does not meet the age requirement. Therefore it must be excluded under E5.

Although this is an fMRI study of face processing (a social perception task) and includes a healthy adult control group, the neuroimaging analyses are conducted as region-of-interest (individual right FFA) analyses rather than reporting group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy/control group. The paper localizes individual FFAs and extracts ROI beta weights/amplitudes for between-group and within-group comparisons; no unmasked, group-level whole-brain activation map for the healthy group is provided. Therefore it does not meet the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task effects and must be excluded.

This study used task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=23, ages 19–32) while they read a narrative and provided suspense ratings. The task probes social-cognitive processes (mentalizing/theory-of-mind and inference about characters), and the authors explicitly interpret activations as related to social cognition (MFC, TPJ). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (second-level random effects SPM results) are reported with cluster- and ROI-corrected statistics and tables/figures of coordinates. Thus the paper provides whole-brain task-evoked maps from a healthy adult sample for a social-related process (perception/understanding of others).

This study used task-based fMRI during social-related processing (thinking about 16 social-interaction items), includes a healthy adult control group (17 age- and IQ-matched controls), and reports group-level within-group whole-brain task contrasts for the control group (all social interactions vs fixation) with associated figures/tables. The healthy participants are adults (young adults) and results for the control group are reported separately from the autism group. Thus it satisfies I3 (fMRI social task), I4 (healthy adult group reported), I5 (whole-brain group-level task-evoked map for controls), and I6 (results presented in text/figures/tables). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only without healthy map, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply.

The study used fMRI with a social-emotional face task and reports whole-brain group maps for controls, but all participant groups are adolescents (ages 12–18) with no healthy adult (18–65) subgroup. This violates the age eligibility requirement. Per exclusion criterion E5, studies that include only participants outside age 18–65 are excluded unless a healthy adult subgroup is reported separately. Therefore the study must be excluded.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social perception (directional head turns) using dynamic social stimuli and MVPA/univariate analyses. Participants are healthy adult volunteers (mean age 29, range 22–38), satisfying the sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain (gray-matter–masked) analyses and corrected whole-volume results (FWE-corrected coordinates and maps) in the main and exploratory analyses, not limited to ROI-only results. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly described and reported (including tables/coordinates and figures). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range sample) apply. Therefore the study meets the inclusion criteria for the review.

This study used task-based fMRI during face perception (socially relevant stimuli), includes a healthy adult control group (n=7, mean age 30 within 18–65), and reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (within-group deactivation maps for task vs. rest and group comparisons) with cluster-correction described. Healthy-control results are reported separately (within-group analysis and comparisons), not limited to ROI or connectivity-only approaches. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults and provides whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps or descriptions of them.

The study is an fMRI investigation of memory for emotional faces, which is a social-related task (perception and understanding of others). Participants are healthy adults (N=35, mean age 29). The paper reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (random-effects ANCOVA, FDR<.05) with Talairach coordinates and whole-brain contrasts (emotion main effect, angry>neutral, load contrasts) clearly reported. Results are not limited to ROIs or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

This is a longitudinal randomized fMRI study using the Ultimatum Game (a social economic exchange task) in healthy adult participants (N=51, ages ~31). The task probes social decision-making/trust/cooperation (social-related processing). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, random-effects task-evoked analyses with voxelwise results (conjunction and interaction contrasts), corrected and uncorrected statistical maps, and coordinates reported in text/tables/supplementary material. Healthy/control group results are clearly described (pre- and post-training whole-brain effects for MT and CT groups). Thus it meets inclusion criteria for a whole-brain fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults.

This is an event-related fMRI study of agency attribution (social cognition/Perception and Understanding of Others) using animated stimuli to evoke intentionality. Participants were healthy adults (n=12, mean age 25.2), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise random-effects analyses (contrasts High>Low and Low>High) with reported activated regions and statistical thresholds (p<0.001 uncorrected). Whole-brain task-evoked results are clearly described in the text and figures. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults and does not violate exclusion criteria.

This study is ineligible for the meta-analysis because it does not use task-based fMRI in healthy adults. It reports resting-state functional connectivity in a clinical sample (male adults with ASD) and examines effects of endogenous and exogenous oxytocin. There is no healthy/control group whole-brain task-evoked activation map: the MRI data are resting-state (intrinsic connectivity) rather than task-evoked, and results pertain to the ASD group; no separate healthy adult group results are reported. Therefore it matches the exclusion criterion for studies reporting only resting-state/seed-based connectivity without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation.

This is a task-based fMRI study of social processing (implicit interpersonal space/affiliation) in healthy adult participants (male, ages 19–30). The paper reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked analyses (main effects and interactions; random-effects GLM with cluster correction) and presents neuroimaging results in the text/figures, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. The sample is within the 18–65 range and results for the healthy group are reported. The study is empirical and not limited to ROI- or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the review are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.

The study used fMRI during a social cognitive (Theory-of-Mind) task but the sample comprises only clinical participants (schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder) with no healthy adult control group and no reported whole-brain task activation map for a healthy/control group. Therefore it does not meet the requirement for inclusion of a healthy adult group (I4) nor provides a healthy-group whole-brain task effect (I5). This violates the review’s eligibility criteria for healthy-group whole-brain task maps. Exclusion applied: E4.

This study used task-based fMRI during social judgement tasks (approachability/intelligence) in healthy adult participants, reporting separate healthy control group results. Group-level whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (social > gender) for healthy males and females are reported, with peak coordinates, thresholding, and figures/tables described. Thus it meets I3 (fMRI social task), I4 (healthy adult group reported separately), I5 (whole-brain group-level voxelwise maps reported), and I6 (results presented in figures/coordinates). No exclusion criteria are violated.

This paper is a tutorial/methods/review article about intersubject correlation (ISC) analysis and related techniques. It does not report original empirical fMRI data from participants, does not describe a specific social-task experiment with a healthy adult sample, and does not present any group-level, whole-brain task activation maps for a healthy/control group. Therefore it does not meet the inclusion criteria requiring original fMRI task data and whole-brain results. Excluded under E6 (non-empirical paper without original fMRI data in healthy adults).

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=25, mean age 25.7) that explicitly probes social-related processing (guilt, social cognition, perspective-taking). The methods report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., guilt memories vs neutral memories) with whole-brain thresholding (p<0.001, cluster extent) and report coordinates/regions; results are presented for the healthy sample. The task involves social scenarios and personal recollections relevant to perception/understanding of others/self. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) apply. Thus it meets all required inclusion criteria for the review.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social-related touch (self vs other touch), which directly addresses social perception and self/other processing. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=30; ages within 18–65) and reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps for the neurotypical controls (e.g., “Other-touch in NC” and self-touch contrasts reported at whole-brain FWE-corrected thresholds). Results for the control group are presented separately and whole-brain effects are clearly described in text and figures. The paper is empirical and uses task-based fMRI rather than only ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3 (fMRI social-related task), I4 (healthy adult sample reported separately), I5 (group-level whole-brain task maps), and I6 (whole-brain results clearly described). No exclusion criteria are met.

This empirical fMRI study includes a social decision-making (altruism) task probing perceptions of others’ outcomes and focus on a partner’s feelings – clearly a social-related construct. Participants are healthy adults (altruism N=55, subset N=37 also did food task; mean age ~28, within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain multivariate searchlight decoding results and cluster coordinates (conjunctions, voxelwise maps, and ROI analyses) showing task-evoked effects; statistical thresholds and MNI coordinates are provided and derived maps are available on OSF. Thus it provides whole-brain, healthy-group task activation/decoding maps relevant to social processing. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state only, non-healthy or out-of-range sample) apply.

This is an fMRI study of social perception (animacy, action observation, theory-of-mind related processes) in healthy adult participants (final N=23, mean age 26.4). The task is social-related (perception and understanding of others), and the paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task activation analyses (voxel-wise threshold p<0.005, cluster correction; peak coordinates and clusters are listed). Results for main effects and interactions are clearly described for the healthy/control group. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for functional MRI social-task data with whole-brain results.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social processing (fearful faces with gaze manipulation), includes a clearly defined healthy adult control group (n=22, ages within 18–65) with results reported separately, and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (within-group contrasts for controls and between-group comparisons) with corrected statistical maps. Thus it meets the meta-analysis requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of social processing (attentional orienting to eye gaze vs arrows with social voice vs tone contexts) in healthy adults (n=22, mean age ~23). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation analyses (main effects and interactions) with appropriate statistical thresholds and tables/figures, and also provides ROI/small-volume correction results. All relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports a task-based fMRI experiment examining audiovisual integration of non-verbal social cues (animated faces and human non-verbal vocalizations), a clear social-related processing paradigm. The fMRI sample includes a healthy adult group (n=10, ages 24–37), satisfying the healthy adult sample requirement. The paper presents group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (voxel-by-voxel parametric t-tests, group activation maps, and cluster-correction procedures) and reports results in figures/tables, meeting the whole-brain evidence criterion. Results for the healthy/control group are reported directly (not limited to a subgroup). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range ages) are violated. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

The study includes healthy adult controls but focuses on seed-based task-dependent functional connectivity (gPPI) analyses and reports between-group comparisons; it does not provide an unmasked, whole-brain group-level task-evoked activation map for the healthy/control group. Therefore it fails to meet the requirement for healthy-group whole-brain task results and must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social cognition task (Theory of Mind; false-belief vs false-photo), satisfying the social-related task requirement. The sample includes a healthy adult control group (n=25) aged 18–59, meeting the 18–65 criterion. The authors report whole-brain, group-level task activation contrasts (FB > FP) and explicitly state they derived functional ROIs/masks from the control group data (i.e., a control-group FB>FP map), with FWE-corrected results and figures/tables referenced; thus whole-brain healthy-group task effects are available. Results are reported in the main text and supplemental materials. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-only, only between-group contrasts without healthy-group task map, out-of-age-range, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6.

Although the study uses fMRI in healthy adult participants and includes social cognition tasks (theory-of-mind and attribution-of-attention), it does not report a group-level, whole-brain (unmasked) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy/control group. The analyses use localized, ROI-based ICA restricted to a temporoparietal mask to identify task-related independent components and report seed-to-voxel connectivity maps, but no unmasked whole-brain voxelwise activation contrast (GLM) is provided. Therefore it constitutes an ROI-focused analysis without whole-brain task activation results, violating the review’s whole-brain evidence requirement.

The study reports task-based fMRI of self- and other-reflection (social cognition: perception/understanding of self and others), includes a healthy adult control group (n=33) aged within 18–65, and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise task activation results for the control group (Self>Facts, Other>Facts, Other>Self) with cluster-level correction. Whole-brain maps and supplementary tables for the control group are described, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. It is empirical fMRI task data (not resting-state or connectivity-only) and healthy-group results are clearly reported separately from the clinical group.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=31 analyzed) investigating social perception of others (neural and behavioural responses to facial disfigurement; relevant to perception/understanding of others and stigma). The fMRI analysis includes group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (SnPM nonparametric group analysis with familywise error correction and cluster-level reporting) comparing pre- vs post-surgery faces, with results presented as whole-brain activation/deactivation clusters. Participant ages (18–35) fall within the 18–65 range. Therefore all inclusion criteria for task-based whole-brain fMRI in healthy adults are met.

Study uses task-based fMRI of prosodic speech perception, which is a social-communication related process (affective/pragmatic prosody). It includes a healthy adult control group (n=8, mean age ~23) reported separately. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses for the control group (one-sample t-tests, conjunctions, and contrasts) with thresholding and anatomical localization. Results for controls are clearly described (activation and deactivation maps). Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study investigates learning about others’ preferences and social influence on inter-temporal choice, using a social-related task (delegated decisions for novel and familiar others) in healthy adult participants (mean ages 23.6 and 25.6; adults 18–65). The paper reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked analyses (random-effects second-level analyses, cluster-defining thresholds and FWE correction) with reported coordinates and figures. Results and contrasts for healthy/control participants are clearly described. Thus it meets all inclusion criteria and violates none.

The study used task-based fMRI during a validated social cognition paradigm (Animated Triangles / HCP social cognition task), includes a clearly reported healthy adult control group (N=25) analyzed separately, and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked activation maps and peak coordinates for the healthy controls (FWE-corrected results and MNI coordinates are provided). Whole-brain results for the healthy group are described in text, figures, and coordinates. Although the paper also reports DCM/effective connectivity and a clinical group, these do not preclude inclusion because the healthy-group whole-brain task effects are explicitly reported. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6.

This study reports task-based fMRI of gesture-speech integration, a social-communication process. It includes healthy adult participant groups (H-group: n=19, ages 19–32; C-group: n=17) reported separately from clinical participants. The paper presents whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task activation results for the healthy/control group (e.g., conjunction and contrasts with MNI coordinates and significance values; Supplementary Table 2), not just ROI or connectivity-only analyses. Thus it satisfies the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults and provides usable whole-brain results.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adults (n=12, ages 20–32) that investigates person-related (social) conceptual processing (learning facts about people vs buildings/hammers). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts and conjunction analyses (person > building AND person > hammer), with cluster-size correction and whole-brain maps and supplemental tables of results and connectivity. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria for an fMRI social-related task (I3), healthy adult sample (I4), whole-brain group-level voxelwise task results (I5), and acceptable reporting of whole-brain results in figures/tables/supplement (I6). No exclusion criteria are met.

The study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (ages 21–48) using erotic picture/video stimuli depicting other people, which falls under social-related constructs (Perception and Understanding of Others). It provides group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation analyses (one-sample contrasts within each healthy orientation group, with FWE-corrected maps and cluster reports) alongside ROI analyses. Whole-brain results are clearly described and presented in figures/tables. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis criteria for fMRI social-related tasks in healthy adults.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in healthy adult participants (ages 18–35), using task-evoked olfactory self-assessment (‘would you like to smell like this?’) that probes perception/understanding of self, a social-related construct. Group-level, within-group (healthy participants) second-level contrasts were conducted (e.g., ‘self’-peptide minus solvent; ‘self’-peptide minus ‘non-self’-peptide) with activation coordinates reported in MNI space (right middle frontal cortex) and statistical thresholds described. The paper states that whole-brain analysis was performed and presents voxelwise activation coordinates and corrected p-values; results are clearly identified for the healthy group. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI of social-related processing in healthy adults and does not violate exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not resting-state, and participants are within 18–65).

The study uses task-based fMRI during a social-norm inference task (social-related processing). It includes a healthy adult control group (22 TD males, ages 18–35) with results reported separately. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts/maps (e.g., all-stimuli vs fixation, visual and auditory GLM contrasts) for the control group and describes statistical results and voxelwise activations. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 and violates no exclusion criteria.

Although this is a task-based fMRI study of personal (social) familiarity and reports whole-brain, group-level activation maps for the healthy control group, the healthy participants are described as "healthy elderly"/older adults rather than adults in the 18–65 range required by the review. No subgroup of healthy participants aged 18–65 is reported separately. Therefore the study violates the age-range inclusion requirement and must be excluded (E5).

This is an empirical fMRI study using a facial emotion discrimination task (socially relevant processing of others’ emotional expressions). Participants are healthy adults aged 19–35 with a clearly defined normal control (NC) group reported separately. The paper reports whole-brain, group-level task activation results (cluster tables and FWE-corrected maps) for within-group contrasts and condition effects in the NC as well as between-group contrasts; ROI results are supplementary but whole-brain voxelwise results for the healthy control group are clearly described. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, includes healthy adult subgroup, empirical fMRI task data).

Although the study used task-based fMRI of social processing (script-driven interpersonal rejection and imagined aggression) and included a healthy adult control group (female adults 18–65), the paper reports whole-brain functional connectivity analyses and group differences in connectivity rather than presenting any group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked activation maps for the healthy/control group. The standard activation results were noted as reported in prior work, but this full text does not provide unmasked healthy-group whole-brain task effects (voxelwise maps or coordinate tables) required by the review. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked healthy-group results and must be excluded.

This study uses task-based fMRI to investigate emotional prosody processing — a social-communication / perception task — in adults. It includes a healthy control group of adults (age range 20–46) reported separately from the ASD group. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task activation analyses (e.g., emotional vs. neutral prosody) with cluster-level FWE correction and reports activations for controls and conjunction maps; results are presented as whole-brain contrasts and coordinates. Although the study also reports PPI effective connectivity, it does not rely solely on ROI or connectivity analyses. Therefore it satisfies the meta-analysis requirements for fMRI social-related task data in healthy adults.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=30, ages 19–39) that investigates social/kinship processing and moral decision-making using movie-viewing and a moral-dilemma task. It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results from both inter-subject correlation (ISC) analyses during movie viewing and a GLM analysis of the moral-decision task, including figures, cluster tables, and unthresholded maps available on NeuroVault. The study population, tasks, and reported whole-brain maps directly address social-related processing in healthy adults and meet the review’s requirements. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social evaluation (perception/understanding of others) in healthy adults (N=20, ages 18–29). The task is social (forced-choice judgments about target persons across situations) and uses task-evoked BOLD fMRI. The paper reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (multilevel whole-brain MLM, cluster coordinates and figures; supplementary tables reported) and ROI follow-ups, satisfying the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, participants are within 18–65, and the paper is empirical). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6.

This is an fMRI study of social evaluation in a healthy adult sample (meets I3 and I4). However, all reported group-level effects were restricted to a bilateral vACC region-of-interest and small-volume–corrected within that ROI. The paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) group-level task activation map or whole-brain coordinates for healthy participants; results focus on ROI-corrected clusters. Therefore it fails the requirement for reporting whole-brain healthy-group task activation and meets exclusion criterion E2 (ROI-only analyses).

The study uses fMRI during a social-related emotional face matching task and includes a healthy adult control group (ages 21–64). However, it does not report an unmasked, whole-brain group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The paper reports whole-brain group×drug interactions and a task activation map collapsed across group and drug (Supplementary Fig. S2), but no standalone voxelwise healthy-group task map or within-control main effect map is presented. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I5 and meets exclusion criterion E4 (reports only between-group contrasts/interactions without an accompanying whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

The study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (male, ages 18–30) performing a social interpersonal-distance task (affiliation/personal space). Whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses are reported (FDR-corrected results, main effects and treatment×protagonist interaction) with regions listed and follow-up ROI analyses. Thus it meets the fMRI social-task requirement, healthy adult sample, and provides whole-brain task activation results described in the text/tables. No exclusion criteria are violated.

This empirical fMRI study used a face-localizer task (faces vs objects/textures) that targets social-related processing (perception/understanding of others). It includes a healthy adult sample (n=51, ages 18–42) reported separately from children. Group-level whole-brain task activation maps for adults were computed and reported (mixed-effects FLAME group maps, contrasts such as Face>Object and Face>Texture, with thresholding and figures/tables). Thus the paper provides whole-brain task-evoked results for healthy adults and meets the review's reporting requirements.

This is an fMRI study using a social-cognitive task (neutral face processing, emotion recognition, affective ToM) in healthy adult participants (N=74), meeting the review’s target population. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task analyses (one-sample t-tests and ANOVA across participants) with whole-brain significance thresholds and results described in text, figures and supplementary tables, not limited to ROI-only findings. Although ROI analyses were also performed, whole-brain task-evoked activations for the healthy/control group are clearly reported. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, out-of-range ages, non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

This study reports task-based functional MRI in healthy adult participants (N=19, ages 18–58) investigating prosody perception/production and its relation to empathy—clearly a social-communication/affective processing task. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts are reported (e.g., “happy-neutral”, “question-neutral”) with correction thresholds and cluster reporting; overlap and SVC results and coordinate tables/figures are described. Behavioral correlations with empathy measures are also reported. All inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria are met.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adults (18–55) using an imitation/observation of emotional faces paradigm — a clearly social-related task. The sample includes a healthy adult group (n=28 initial, n=20 analyzed) within the 18–65 range. The paper presents group-level, whole-brain analyses: spatio-temporal PLS voxel maps (bootstrap-ratio thresholded) and a complementary whole-brain GLM in SPM8, with voxelwise results displayed and described. Results are not limited to ROIs or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

This empirical fMRI study used a social-related task (anticipation of touching an animate versus inanimate target), recruiting healthy adult participants aged 21–33, and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked analyses (paired-sample t-tests and covariate analyses) with FDR-corrected results and coordinates/figures. Resting-state analyses are present but are accompanied by whole-brain task results. Thus it satisfies all inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6) and violates no exclusion criteria.

The study meets several inclusion points (fMRI social task; healthy adult control group present) but does not report an unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task activation map or within-group main effect for the control group. The reported whole-brain results are group-by-empathy interaction and between-group differences; no clear voxelwise healthy-control task map (main effect or within-group contrast) is provided in the text. This falls under exclusion criterion E4 (only between-group/interactions reported without an accompanying whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

This study used task-based fMRI (Cyberball social exclusion), includes a healthy adult control group (HC; n=28) reported separately, and reports whole-brain, group-level task-evoked results for the healthy controls (one-way ANOVA main effect of condition in HC) with voxelwise FWE-corrected maps and coordinates/figures. The task probes social exclusion (a social-related construct). Healthy participants are adults (female-only sample) and results for the HC group are clearly described. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 are satisfied.

Although the study uses task-based fMRI of a social paradigm (empathy-for-pain) and includes a healthy adult control group, the full text does not clearly report a within-control-group, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map that is unambiguously identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The reported whole-brain analyses appear to focus on alexithymia-based subgroups and group comparisons, and the text describes a between-group contrast (control vs. autism) but does not present an unmasked, whole-brain control-group task effect. Because the review requires at least one clearly reported whole-brain healthy-group task map, this study fails inclusion criterion I5 and therefore must be excluded under E4 (reports only between-group contrasts/subgroup analyses without an accompanying unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

The study reports an fMRI task (modified Empathic Accuracy Task) that probes perception and understanding of others’ emotions (a social-related construct). The sample consists of a healthy adult group (n=34, ages 20–30) reported separately. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked contrasts (emotional > neutral, happy > sad, parametric modulation by empathic accuracy, and time-series correlations with continuous ratings) are reported with TFCE/FWE correction and peak coordinates/tables. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly described. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met (I3, I4, I5, I6).

The study uses fMRI during social-related tasks (action observation/understanding) and includes a healthy control group, but it does not report an unmasked, whole-brain group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group (e.g., HC within-group main effect or HC understand>observe map). The imaging results presented are primarily between-group contrasts (ALS > HC and HC > ALS). According to the review criteria, studies that report only between-group contrasts without an accompanying unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task effect must be excluded (E4). Although inclusion criteria I3 and I4 are met, the lack of a reported whole-brain healthy-group task map violates I5 and triggers exclusion under E4.

Although the study includes a healthy adult control group and uses task-based fMRI examining self-related (agency) processing (relevant to social-related constructs), it does not provide a usable whole-brain, group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group. The authors report ROI analyses showing activation in frontal ROIs for controls, but whole-brain analyses yielded no significant activations and no whole-brain coordinates or maps for the healthy group are reported. Therefore the paper effectively reports only ROI-based results (and between-group ROI contrasts) without an accompanying unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect, failing the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked maps.

Although the study uses task-based fMRI with healthy control participants and examines socially relevant emotion-word processing, the paper does not report an unmasked, whole-brain group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The reported whole-brain results are primarily pooled across all participants or presented as between-group contrasts (controls > ASC) and ROI analyses. Per the review criteria, studies that present only between-group contrasts without an accompanying unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task effect must be excluded (E4). Therefore this study is excluded for failing to provide a standalone healthy-group whole-brain task map.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=60 males, mean age 23.8), using an impression-formation task involving social perception of faces varying in race and socioeconomic status — a social-related construct (perception and understanding of others). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level task analyses (GLM contrast images used for PLS; voxelwise whole-brain results with cluster reporting and coordinates identified via xjview) and presents whole-brain PLS results and clusters. Results for the healthy adult sample are reported directly and are not restricted to a narrow subgroup. Thus the study meets the review’s inclusion criteria for task fMRI in healthy adults with whole-brain task-evoked maps. Inclusion criteria satisfied: I3, I4, I5, I6.

This is an fMRI study of social gaze processing using a task with virtual characters (social-related processing). The sample is healthy adults (N=30 after exclusions; ages 19–41). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked analyses (second-level flexible factorial contrasts; cluster-forming threshold p<0.001 and FWE cluster correction) with reported coordinates and figures. Whole-brain results are clearly described for the healthy participant group. Although the paper also reports PPI connectivity, it additionally provides unmasked whole-brain task activation maps and coordinate tables. Thus all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria are violated.

The paper reports fMRI during clearly social-related tasks (theory of mind ‘Reading the Mind in the Eyes’ and basic emotion tasks) and includes a healthy adult control group reported separately (n=14). The authors conducted and report group-level, whole-brain regression analyses for each group (controls, patients, siblings) with thresholding and report activated regions as well as MNI coordinates and laterality indices. Whole-brain results for the healthy/control group are described in the text (and in tables/coordinates), satisfying the requirement for unmasked, group-level task-evoked maps. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only or connectivity-only reporting) apply.

While this fMRI study examines social gaze processing and includes a healthy adult control group, it does not provide a clearly identified, unmasked whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The reported group results focus on group × gaze-direction interactions and ROI-based small-volume corrected effects within a priori ToM regions; the within-group healthy/control effects are presented in the context of ROI analyses or interactions rather than as an unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task map. Whole-brain peaks cited for motor/visual networks appear to be from contrasts across subjects and are not clearly reported as a standalone healthy-group whole-brain activation map. Therefore the paper matches exclusion criterion E4 (between-group contrasts/interactions without an accompanying unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

This study used task-based fMRI with a social contingency (pseudo-interactive joke) paradigm and includes a healthy neurotypical adult control group; however, the paper reports only a region-of-interest (ROI) analysis focused on the anterior rostral MPFC and explicitly states that whole-brain and functional connectivity analyses could not be conducted due to signal loss. No group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked activation maps for the healthy/control group are reported. Therefore it fails the whole-brain evidence requirement for inclusion.

This fMRI study investigates face perception and social/emotional processing (mentalizing, eye-region attention) using the Thatcher Illusion, a social-related task. It includes a healthy adult control group (NT; n=18, mean age 25.8±5.3) reported separately from the ASD group. The paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked contrasts for the NT group (within-group whole-brain activation maps, thresholded and described in text/figures/tables). Therefore it meets the meta-analysis requirements for fMRI social-related task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain healthy-group results.

The study uses fMRI during a social perception task (trustworthiness/fear appraisal) and includes a healthy adult control group (ages 18–45). However, the paper does not clearly report a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map that is explicitly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. Reported whole-brain results appear to be across all participants or between-group contrasts, and control-group results are reported mainly via ROI analyses and statistics rather than an unmasked whole-brain healthy-group map. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I5 and meets exclusion criterion E4.

The study uses task-based fMRI of gesture pantomime, a social communication task (social action planning). It includes a healthy adult control group (n=25) and reports whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked analyses with within-group (control) results noted (within-group results and tables/figures provided in supplementary material). Analyses used SPM8 whole-brain contrasts and report thresholds and cluster sizes, satisfying requirements for group-level whole-brain maps for the healthy group. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, no healthy group whole-brain map, or out-of-range ages) appear to apply.

While the study uses fMRI of social-related face processing (meets I3) and includes healthy adult participants (meets I4), it does not provide a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. The primary whole-brain genome-wide analyses combined healthy controls and psychiatric participants, and although the authors report no effect of diagnosis and perform covariate analyses, they do not present an unambiguous healthy-group whole-brain activation map. The independent replication used an ROI approach in healthy volunteers rather than whole-brain healthy-group maps. Therefore the paper fails inclusion criterion I5 and must be excluded under E4.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (parents aged 22–37) using socially relevant, attachment-related stimuli (own-infant vs. standard-infant videos). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (second-level GLM, whole-brain intersubject correlations, cluster locations, thresholds, and ROI follow-up), with results clearly identified for the healthy adult group. Although the sample is modest (n=30) and some analyses are exploratory with liberal thresholds, all required inclusion criteria are met: fMRI social task (I3), healthy adult sample 18–65 (I4), and whole-brain group-level task-evoked maps reported (I5, I6). No exclusion criteria apply.

This study used task-based fMRI during an implicit emotional face task (angry vs neutral faces), which is a social-perception/understanding-of-others paradigm. A healthy adult control group (ages reported within 18–65, n=23 for the fMRI cohort) is analyzed separately. The methods describe voxelwise, whole-brain second-level GLM analyses (first-level contrasts entered into second-level analyses) and report task-activated brain regions (with further details in the supplementary material), meeting the requirement for a group-level whole-brain task-evoked map for controls. Connectivity (PPI) was also performed but the paper includes whole-brain activation analyses rather than only ROI/seed analyses. Therefore the paper meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults.

The study uses fMRI during a social (joint attention) task with healthy adult participants (meets I3 and I4). However, it does not report any group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy group. The paper focuses on ROI-based hyperscanning directed functional connectivity analyses (4-region networks, predefined cortical masks) and probabilistic counts of regional occurrences rather than univariate whole-brain activation results. Therefore it violates inclusion criterion I5 and meets exclusion criteria for studies that present only ROI/connectivity analyses without a whole-brain healthy-group task map.

This is a task-based fMRI study of eye-gaze perception (a social-processing construct) in a sample of healthy adults (ages 18–30). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level second-level analyses (voxelwise SPM-t maps) testing contrasts (variable vs. constant gaze/heads/eyes-only) with AQ as a regressor, thresholded with whole-brain FDR and confirmed in ROI SVC — and coordinates of significant clusters are reported. Thus it meets social-task fMRI (I3), healthy adult sample (I4), whole-brain group-level task-evoked maps clearly from the healthy group (I5), and reporting of whole-brain results via coordinates/tables (I6). No exclusion criteria apply.

This study used task-based fMRI during a social-related approach-avoidance (AA) task comparing social versus nonsocial stimuli (meets social-processing requirement). Participants were healthy adults (male, mean age 21.35) with results reported separately for treatment groups of healthy subjects. The manuscript reports group-level task analyses and explicitly states exploratory whole-brain results were performed and reported (in main text/supplement), and contrasts are clearly identified at the group level. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria for fMRI social task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain group-level reporting.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (perception of infant cries and faces—attachment/affiliation and social perception) in healthy adult participants. The sample consists of 17 healthy nulliparous women aged 19–29. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked contrasts (e.g., cry vs. pink noise; happy vs. neutral faces) with cluster- and FWE-correction and provides coordinate tables/figures and whole-brain correlation analyses. Thus all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study used resting-state fMRI with a social-evaluation manipulation (critical remarks) and reports seed-based functional connectivity contrasts (criticism > standard) and clustering results. Although the sample consists of healthy adults (age 18–27) and the paradigm involves social-related processing, the paper does not report any group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked activation maps from a standard task analysis. Results are limited to seed-based connectivity and resting-state contrasts. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E3 (studies reporting only seed-based connectivity/resting-state analyses without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map).

Although the study uses task-based fMRI of face processing (a social perception task) in healthy adult participants (meets I3 and I4), it does not report any group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy/control group. Analyses are ROI-based interregional correlations and structural covariance rather than whole-brain voxelwise activation results. Therefore it violates the requirement for whole-brain task evidence (I5) and falls under exclusion criterion E2 (reports only ROI/region-based analyses with no whole-brain results).

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-emotional approach-avoidance task (social-related processing) in a sample of healthy adults (N=279, age 18–43). The paper reports group-level task-evoked analyses, including whole-brain contrasts (congruency effects and stress-response-related whole-brain results) and clearly describes these as coming from the healthy/control group. Results are reported with whole-brain correction and ROI SVC, and coordinate/cluster-level findings are provided. All inclusion criteria for the review (task is social-related fMRI, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain group-level task maps reported) are satisfied. No exclusion criteria apply.

The paper reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (three studies, total n=59 controls) performing social-related tasks (person knowledge, famous names, socially relevant concept words) contrasted against non-social semantic conditions and active baselines. Group-level, whole-brain second-level analyses (one-way ANOVAs and contrasts such as social > non-social) are reported, with peak coordinates and whole-brain results described and shown. Results for the healthy/control group are presented separately and clearly. Reporting of voxelwise task-evoked maps and coordinate tables/figures satisfies whole-brain evidence requirements. Therefore all inclusion criteria for empirical task-based fMRI in healthy adults with whole-brain group results are met.

This study reports a task-based fMRI experiment examining audiovisual integration of non-verbal social cues (animated faces and human non-verbal vocalizations), a clear social-related processing paradigm. The fMRI sample includes a healthy adult group (n=10, ages 24–37), satisfying the healthy adult sample requirement. The paper presents group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (voxel-by-voxel parametric t-tests, group activation maps, and cluster-correction procedures) and reports results in figures/tables, meeting the whole-brain evidence criterion. Results for the healthy/control group are reported directly (not limited to a subgroup). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range ages) are violated. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

This study reports task-based functional MRI in healthy adult participants (N=19, ages 18–58) investigating prosody perception/production and its relation to empathy—clearly a social-communication/affective processing task. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts are reported (e.g., “happy-neutral”, “question-neutral”) with correction thresholds and cluster reporting; overlap and SVC results and coordinate tables/figures are described. Behavioral correlations with empathy measures are also reported. All inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria are met.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=25, mean age 25.7) that explicitly probes social-related processing (guilt, social cognition, perspective-taking). The methods report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., guilt memories vs neutral memories) with whole-brain thresholding (p<0.001, cluster extent) and report coordinates/regions; results are presented for the healthy sample. The task involves social scenarios and personal recollections relevant to perception/understanding of others/self. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) apply. Thus it meets all required inclusion criteria for the review.

This is a longitudinal randomized fMRI study using the Ultimatum Game (a social economic exchange task) in healthy adult participants (N=51, ages ~31). The task probes social decision-making/trust/cooperation (social-related processing). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, random-effects task-evoked analyses with voxelwise results (conjunction and interaction contrasts), corrected and uncorrected statistical maps, and coordinates reported in text/tables/supplementary material. Healthy/control group results are clearly described (pre- and post-training whole-brain effects for MT and CT groups). Thus it meets inclusion criteria for a whole-brain fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults.

Although the study uses fMRI in healthy adult participants and includes social cognition tasks (theory-of-mind and attribution-of-attention), it does not report a group-level, whole-brain (unmasked) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy/control group. The analyses use localized, ROI-based ICA restricted to a temporoparietal mask to identify task-related independent components and report seed-to-voxel connectivity maps, but no unmasked whole-brain voxelwise activation contrast (GLM) is provided. Therefore it constitutes an ROI-focused analysis without whole-brain task activation results, violating the review’s whole-brain evidence requirement.

Although the study uses fMRI during a social-related face encoding/recognition task and includes healthy adult participants, all reported neuroimaging analyses focus on an a priori amygdala ROI (parameter estimates extracted via MarsBaR) and the paper does not report any group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation maps for the healthy group. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain evidence and meets exclusion criterion E2 (ROI-only analyses).

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adults (18–55) using an imitation/observation of emotional faces paradigm — a clearly social-related task. The sample includes a healthy adult group (n=28 initial, n=20 analyzed) within the 18–65 range. The paper presents group-level, whole-brain analyses: spatio-temporal PLS voxel maps (bootstrap-ratio thresholded) and a complementary whole-brain GLM in SPM8, with voxelwise results displayed and described. Results are not limited to ROIs or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=30, ages 19–39) that investigates social/kinship processing and moral decision-making using movie-viewing and a moral-dilemma task. It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results from both inter-subject correlation (ISC) analyses during movie viewing and a GLM analysis of the moral-decision task, including figures, cluster tables, and unthresholded maps available on NeuroVault. The study population, tasks, and reported whole-brain maps directly address social-related processing in healthy adults and meet the review’s requirements. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply.

This is an fMRI study of social evaluation in a healthy adult sample (meets I3 and I4). However, all reported group-level effects were restricted to a bilateral vACC region-of-interest and small-volume–corrected within that ROI. The paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) group-level task activation map or whole-brain coordinates for healthy participants; results focus on ROI-corrected clusters. Therefore it fails the requirement for reporting whole-brain healthy-group task activation and meets exclusion criterion E2 (ROI-only analyses).

The study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (ages 21–48) using erotic picture/video stimuli depicting other people, which falls under social-related constructs (Perception and Understanding of Others). It provides group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation analyses (one-sample contrasts within each healthy orientation group, with FWE-corrected maps and cluster reports) alongside ROI analyses. Whole-brain results are clearly described and presented in figures/tables. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis criteria for fMRI social-related tasks in healthy adults.

This is an fMRI study of social interaction perception in healthy adult participants (ages 18–34 across experiments). The paper reports group-level whole-brain analyses (surface-based random effects group analysis and whole-brain contrasts with FDR correction) identifying pSTS clusters for interaction > non-interaction, satisfying whole-brain reporting. The tasks probe social-related processing (perception/understanding of others) using task-evoked fMRI. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study reports an fMRI task (modified Empathic Accuracy Task) that probes perception and understanding of others’ emotions (a social-related construct). The sample consists of a healthy adult group (n=34, ages 20–30) reported separately. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked contrasts (emotional > neutral, happy > sad, parametric modulation by empathic accuracy, and time-series correlations with continuous ratings) are reported with TFCE/FWE correction and peak coordinates/tables.
